author: blu
body: `macros`, `serial-mirror` and `serial-remote` are in the design's record. This chapter used to say they would move in here once their modules existed. Both modules landed on 2026-07-28 and neither field did, and that is a decision rather than an omission.

author: blu
body: `Macro.codex` owns its own `MacroTable`, because a macro table is data with its own bounds, refusals and splitter, and a chapter that owns them can be tested as a unit -- which is the same argument that put the watch table here rather than in `MemInspector`. The two serial flags stayed in the console's own record because they are not debugger DATA at all: they govern how the console does I/O, and nothing pure has an opinion about them.

author: blu
body: `last-result` is in the design's record too, and it is left out for a different and stronger reason: **the console already has it.** The debugger's `last-address` is what an evaluated expression sets and what `$` reads, and it has been that since ExprEval landed. Adding a second field holding the same number would make two places that must agree and nothing that checks they do -- which is the shape of the three direction constants, the three partition GUIDs, and every other duplicated fact this project has had to go back and derive instead. One value, one home.

author: blu
body: THE WHOLE THING IS PURE. `peek-byte` carries no effect row, so taking a snapshot and comparing one are ordinary functions and this chapter can be tested without a machine. That is not an accident of the builtin: it is why the watch logic lives here rather than in the console, which cannot be tested without one.

author: blu
body: PURE INCLUDES NOT MUTATING THE STATE HANDED IN, and the first cut of this chapter failed that while claiming it. Every state transition built its result with `__record-set st "ds-watches" ...`, which stores into the field and returns THE SAME record, so a caller that kept its own `st` found the new watch in it. Two CDX6020 warnings said so, at the two constructors.

author: blu
body: A refusal says which cap was hit. Silently dropping the thirty-third watch would leave an operator watching something they believe they are not.

author: blu
body: IT CANNOT SAY WHAT CHANGED, and that is a real limit rather than an oversight. Storing the bytes would allow an old-against-new diff and cost the region's length per watch; a checksum costs one integer. The dump is one command away (`dbg mem <addr>`), so the pairing is: this tells you THAT it moved, and MemInspector shows you what it is now. If a future reader wants the diff, the honest change is storing bytes under a small per-watch cap, not widening this.

author: blu
body: A check RE-SNAPSHOTS every watch it reports. Without that, one change makes a watch report as changed on every check for the rest of the session, and an operator watching two regions cannot tell which one moved this time. Re-arming means each report answers "since the last check", which is the question being asked.

author: blu
body: The report names the unchanged watches too. A checker that prints only what moved is silent when nothing does, and silence reads the same as a watch list that was never armed.
